extracted.intended_audience: educators, education theorists, teachers, and policymakers interested in progressive education theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles and standards for educating children from a philosophical/psychological account of learning and social formation (Dewey-style). Useful for designing curricula, pedagogical environments, and evaluating whether schooling fosters socialized intelligence and growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning arises from use in action
rubrics_metrics.description: An object's meaning is supplied by the specific use to which it is put rather than by mere aggregated sensations (color, shape, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a chair's meaning comes from being used for sitting; an orange's meaning from being eaten and its taste/smell. Implication: teaching should connect objects/ideas to their instrumental uses, not present them as isolated sensory data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental act vs. blind adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: A mental response involves responding to a thing in its meaning (intentional, foresightful), whereas a mere physical adjustment is a blind, unconscious reaction to stimuli.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: running to put out a blaze (intelligent) vs. jumping at a noise (physical). Anti-pattern: confusing conditioned/automatic responses with genuine understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education differs from training/habit formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Training or repeated physical responses may form habits without educating because they lack conscious purpose and understanding of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a child forced to bow by neck pressure may form the habit of bowing but not the understanding or intention behind it. Criterion for education: the pupil performs acts with knowledge of their meaning and ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared activity produces common understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine social intercourse and common mind arise when each participant refers his actions to the actions and consequences of others, creating a common intent and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexample: multiple workers contributing to a product without awareness of others' roles produce no social intelligence. Example: a ball game requires mutual awareness and adapting actions to sustain the game.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social control is intellectual, not merely personal/moral
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief means of social control are habits of understanding established through joint use of objects and shared activities, not direct personal coercion or moral exhortation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: sustainable behavioral change comes from organizing situations that instantiate common ends and shared uses, rather than from commands, threats, or isolated moral instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive movements become meaningful through social use
rubrics_metrics.description: Organic expressions (blushing, gestures) are not inherently expressive but are used by others as signs to guide responsive action; their meaning depends on socially shared interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a frown signals possible rebuke; a distant person's waving arms may be meaningless unless interest/concern makes it a sign. Instruction: teach pupils to interpret and act on socially relevant signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language is central but must be grounded in shared activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Language condenses and transmits social meanings and past experience, enabling vicarious participation, but it is most effective when connected to tangible cooperative activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: overreliance on 'telling' and bookish instruction detaches language from its use. Recommendation: integrate verbal instruction with practical shared tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation is subordinate to purposive shared activity
rubrics_metrics.description: What is called 'imitation' often misnames participation in a joint situation; imitation of means (to achieve ends) is intelligent, while imitation of ends without understanding is superficial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: children may mimic outward acts (mere mimicry) but this does not form dispositions. Effective pedagogy promotes imitation of useful methods embedded in purposeful activity, not rote mimicry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional education requires a specially selected environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Education must provide an environment intentionally equipped with materials and methods that promote desired growth and cooperative uses of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schools need physical tools and apparatus enabling direct occupations with things; otherwise theory (active, constructive learning) cannot be enacted. Anti-pattern: preaching active learning while lacking resources to do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schools must prioritize conjoint/ cooperative activities
rubrics_metrics.description: To develop social intelligence and dispositions, schools should organize opportunities for joint activities where students' uses of materials are consciously referred to others' actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conjoint tasks foster a social sense of one's powers and of materials; avoiding such tasks produces a 'bookish, pseudo-intellectual spirit' that undermines social understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid isolated intellectual learning as primary aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating learning as a separate, conscious business (purely bookish) tends to preclude the social sense and undermines intelligence directed toward useful ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: couple intellectual instruction with shared activities and practical occupations. Anti-patterns: curricula that separate classroom study from collaborative, applied activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immutability of immaturity: see immaturity as positive capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Imaturity should be understood not as mere lack but as a positive power or capacity to grow; growth is something the young do, not something simply done to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design education that fosters the child's active constructive tendencies. Avoid measuring childhood only as deficit relative to adult standards, which risks stifling child's positive powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence as constructive power/interdependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Children's dependence is a positive, constructive power (interdependence) that enables social development and elicits nurturing and cooperative responses from adults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for pedagogy: care and joint activity around dependent learners stimulate affectionate watchfulness and social habits; overemphasis on early self-reliance may reduce social capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plasticity: capacity to learn and transfer methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Plasticity denotes the ability to retain factors from prior experience and carry them over to modify subsequent activities—i.e., the power to learn, form habits, and develop dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with animals with fixed instincts; human infants' tentative reactions enable varied combinations and the habit of learning. Pedagogical implication: provide varied experiences that encourage transferable methods and the 'habit of learning.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolonged infancy supports social and intellectual development
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended period of childhood/dependence provides stimuli for nurturing, affection, foresight, planning, and learning to learn, which in turn propel social progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: recognize social and evolutionary value of prolonged childhood; design schooling and social institutions that capitalize on this prolonged plasticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habits as executive skills and expressions of growth
rubrics_metrics.description: A habit is an ability to use natural conditions as means to ends—an executive skill reflecting growth and efficiency in doing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational aim: cultivate habits that coordinate body control and use of environment toward purposeful ends. Note: habits formed without meaning are inadequate; aim for habits that embody understanding and instrumental competence.
